title-group.article-title: Fiducial-marked laminectomy window for intrathecal medication administration after spinal fusion: illustrative case

sec.title: BACKGROUND
sec.p: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is an inherited disease that leads to weakness, loss of ambulation, and progressive scoliosis in many patients, frequently requiring early spinal fusion. Nusinersen is a disease-modifying agent that improves symptoms and slows the progression of SMA but requires serial lumbar punctures for intrathecal drug delivery. Spinal fusion for scoliosis has historically been a contraindication for nusinersen therapy, as the fused spinal laminae block access to the thecal sac.

sec.title: OBSERVATIONS
sec.p: Here, the authors report a case wherein a patient with SMA and prior scoliosis surgery underwent a one-level lumbar laminectomy with the placement of four titanium microscrews at the corners of the bone window thatfunction as fiducial targets for radiography-guided lumbar punctures. This procedure allowed the patient to receive nusinersen injections easily and successfully on an ongoing basis.

sec.title: LESSONS
sec.p: Nusinersen is an important novel treatment for children with SMA. Thus, it is imperative to discover new ways to administer intrathecal injections to increase the number of patients able to undergo this therapy. The described one-level laminectomy with microscrew placement for serial lumbar punctures can increase the number of patients able to receive nusinersen and other intrathecal therapies.
Keywords: laminectomy, nusinersen, intrathecal therapy, spinal muscular atrophy, SMA, scoliosis, case report
ABBREVIATIONS: AP = anteroposterior, CT = computed tomography, IR = interventional radiology, MRI = magnetic resonance imaging, SMA = spinal muscular atrophy.

body.p: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a hereditary protein deficiency that leads to progressive loss of motor function and strength in the chronic forms (types 2 and 3) or early death in type 1. Depending on the subtype, 60%–100% of patients with SMA develop scoliosis, progressing 5°–15° per year, and bracing is usually not well tolerated.1–3 In patients with neuromuscular diseases, scoliosis usually develops at an earlier age, is more rapidly progressive, and responds poorly to nonsurgical treatment.4 Severe scoliosis can cause restrictive lung disease, pressure ulcers, difficulty with sitting upright, nutritional deficiencies, pain, and other challenges. As a result, a high percentage of patients with SMA undergo surgical spinal fusion treatment for scoliosis.

Nusinersen (Spinraza, Biogen) is a disease-modifying agent that requires intrathecal administration with four initial injections as a loading dose and maintenance dose injections every 4 months.1 Spinal fusion surgery has been considered a contraindication to nusinersen therapy, as it becomes increasingly difficult to access the intrathecal space through the sclerotic fused posterior spine. This leaves a significant portion of the otherwise eligible patient population unable to receive this therapy. While there are a few alternatives to serial lumbar spinal punctures, such as cervical puncture,5 a transforaminal approach to lumbar puncture,6, 7 or subcutaneous intrathecal catheter placement,8 these options are typically more complex to perform and are associated with a higher risk of postprocedure complications than standard interventional radiology (IR)–guided lumbar punctures. Thus, it is important to determine alternative methods of thecal sac access so that all qualifying patients with SMA have the potential to receive this disease-altering medication.

In this case report, we describe a method of posterior laminectomy with microscrew fiducial marker placement to delineate a space for ongoing lumbar punctures for intrathecal nusinersen therapy in a young patient with SMA who had undergone previous scoliosis spinal fusion.

sec.title: Illustrative Case
sec.p: A teenage boy with infantile-onset SMA underwent spinal fusion surgery for scoliotic deformity. He began receiving nusinersen therapy via lumbar punctures performed by the IR team approximately 6 years later. This significantly improved his disease symptoms, but it became increasingly difficult to administer due to a large bony fusion mass forming in his lumbar spine. On a repeat computed tomography (CT) scan, a tiny bony gap was identified that could have been used for punctures in the future but would have required CT imaging guidance for each access, significantly increasing his lifetime radiation exposure. He was referred for neurosurgical evaluation for possible intrathecal port placement about 1 year after initiating nusinersen therapy.

Unfortunately, there are currently no Food and Drug Administration–approved intrathecal port systems available in the United States. Off-label use of an intrathecal infusion pump system was considered but was believed to be suboptimal, as these are large implants and not intended for use with nusinersen. Thus, we proposed a one-level laminectomy to provide direct access to the thecal sac for future therapeutic lumbar punctures and to permanently mark the laminectomy site for easy localization in the future.

The surgery was timed approximately 2 weeks after a nusinersen injection to allow at least 3 months of healing prior to the next injection. Intraoperatively, fluoroscopy was used to identify the L4 lamina, and a laminectomy was performed to expose a 2-cm region of thecal sac. The edges of the exposed bones were coated with bone wax to discourage future bone growth across the window. Multiple layers of Gelfoam were placed over the thecal sac to protect the dura and further inhibit bony ingrowth. Four titanium microscrews (MatrixNEURO, DePuy Synthes), which are normally used for craniofacial plating and are magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) compatible to 3.0T, were then placed into the bone at the corners of the laminectomy window. Postoperative radiographic images were obtained to confirm placement and adequate visualization for future procedures (Fig. 1). The patient went home on the same day and had an uneventful recovery.

caption.p: Postoperative lumbar radiograph confirming visualization of microscrew fiducials demarcating the thecal access window.

sec.p: The first dose of nusinersen was injected 14 weeks after the procedure, after radiography and MRI of the lumbar spine confirmed adequate healing in the region. Anteroposterior (AP) and lateral fluoroscopy images were obtained to confirm intrathecal placement of the needle prior to injection (Fig. 2). In the 3 years he continued to be treated at our institution, he received regular fluoroscopy-guided intrathecal injections through the fiducial window without any incidents or complications.

caption.p: A: AP localization of the lumbar puncture site using microscrew fiducial markers to delineate the bony access window to the thecal sac. B: Lateral view of the needle to ensure intrathecal placement prior to injection.

sec.title: Informed Consent
sec.p: The necessary informed consent was obtained in this study.

sec.title: Observations
sec.p: In patients with SMA, nusinersen therapy has been shown to improve muscle strength, the achievement of motor milestones, and ventilator-free survival.9–11 However, many patients with SMA undergo spinal fusion surgery for progressive scoliotic deformity, making it increasingly difficult to access the thecal sac via lumbar puncture as the lumbar spine continues to fuse. Identifying methods of administering intrathecal therapy to those who have undergone scoliosis fusion surgery will increase the number of patients who are eligible for this life-altering treatment. However, the validity of prior spinal fusion as a relative contraindication to intrathecal injection therapy is questionable, and the potential benefit of such therapies is high for patients who would otherwise be candidates.

To our knowledge, this is only the second report of any method of laminectomy to increase the ease of access for serial lumbar punctures in patients with SMA. In a previous report from 2019, a five-patient case series was described wherein the surgeon performed an L3–4 laminectomy with fat graft placement to prevent future bony fusion. In two of the cases, hemoclips were placed on the spinous process of the level above and level below for future imaging guidance. In all cases, a tattoo was also placed on the skin after closing the incision to provide an external landmark for the laminectomy site.1 The individual nature of case reports can limit the generalizability of this technique, and we have not had the opportunity to compare this method head-to-head with the previously published technique. However, we believe that the four-screw fiducial method described here offers distinct advantages, as the screws are smaller in profile and better delineate the region for lumbar puncture by forming a box on fluoroscopic imaging, thus providing two-dimensional guidance for later fluoroscopic lumbar punctures. This technique also negates the need for tattooing the patient. This technical advance requires further validation prior to its institution as standard-of-care in patients needing intrathecal therapy in SMA. However, our patient had an excellent outcome and continued to receive intrathecal nusinersen therapy more than 3 years after the operation, without complications.

sec.title: Lessons
sec.p: Here, we describe a novel procedure to provide a bony window through which intrathecal therapy can be administered. In this procedure, small craniofacial fixation bone screws are placed around the laminectomy window as markers for image-guided lumbar punctures, making continued access rapid and reliable. An advantage of this method is that it can be performed either during the initial scoliosis surgery or in patients who have undergone prior surgery and have prior fusion, thus offering the potential for nusinersen therapy in a patient population for whom, up until this time, it has been considered contraindicated. Given the positive outcomes of many patients receiving nusinersen treatment, we hope that the surgical method described here will increase the cohort of patients who are eligible for this therapy and improve the ease of intrathecal access for many children experiencing this devastating disease. This technique can also be generalized for other patients requiring intrathecal access for testing or treatment who have undergone prior lumbar fusion surgery.
